title: A Pentecostal service
hook: long praise, open prayer, testimony, altar call

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Quaker meeting: a still small voice, and silence closing back over. Your line was the gathered silence.

The drummer counts in, and the room is already on its feet. A song starts and keeps going, the same chorus again and again, louder, then softer, then louder. Hands go up all over the room. A woman near the front is crying, and smiling. Somebody shouts amen in the middle of a line. Then the pastor says, let's pray, and the whole room prays out loud at once, every voice saying something different, a wave of sound. Yesterday's room waited in silence. This one waits with everything it's got.
screen: `THE ROOM IS ALREADY ON ITS FEET.`

segments.voice: Pentecostal churches take their name from a day in the book of Acts. The followers of Jesus are together in one place. "And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting." Then "they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Pentecostals expect that same Spirit in the room today. First, long praise: not one hymn but a stretch of singing, often with hands raised, sometimes with dancing. A psalm gives the reason: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Second, open prayer: many voices praying aloud together, and some praying in tongues, a prayer language they understand as a gift of the Spirit. Other Christians understand the gift of tongues differently, and some believe it belonged to the earliest church. Pentecostals hold that it's for now. Third, testimony. Someone stands and tells what God has done for them this week: a healing, a job, a night they didn't drink. Ordinary people with a microphone, telling the truth. Fourth, the altar call. Near the end, the pastor invites anyone who wants prayer, or wants to give their life to Christ, to come to the front, and others gather round, lay hands on them and pray. Behind it all stands a line Jesus said to Nicodemus: "The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit." Wind you can hear, but can't hold.
screen: `A ROOM, A WIND, AND OTHER TONGUES.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a song of praise from any church you like; if not, hum, or breathe out slowly a few times. Let your body join in somehow, hands open on your knees or lifted a little, whatever feels honest. If you pray, thank God out loud for one thing; if not, say aloud one thing you're glad of today.
A Pentecostal service. Worship named for the day of Pentecost, expecting the Spirit to move in the room.
Your line: the spirit moves. Everything that has breath gets to join in. Day one thousand three hundred forty.

howItsDone: Pentecostal and charismatic churches typically hold long times of sung praise with raised hands, open prayer in which some pray in tongues, testimonies from members and an altar call inviting people forward for prayer.

original.note: Greek: wind, breath, spirit — John 3:8 plays on it, so the wind that blows and the Spirit are one word.

what it means: worship that expects the Spirit of Pentecost in the room: long praise, open prayer, testimony, an altar call.
what a scholar hears: in John 3:8 the Greek pneuma means both wind and spirit, so Jesus's line about the wind is also a line about the Spirit.

chat.says: I visited a Pentecostal church and everyone prayed out loud at once. Is that normal there?
options: Yes. Pentecostals expect the Spirit to move, as at Pentecost, so prayer is open and loud.
No. That only happens once a year, on the feast day the church is named after.
No. It was likely a mistake; Pentecostal services are usually silent and still.

notes: Editor: cut 'Twenty minutes in', an unsourced number that also echoed yesterday's 'twenty people'.

Speaking in tongues: Pentecostals (continuationist) hold the gift is for today; some other Christians (cessationist) hold it belonged to the apostolic age; others hold views in between. Stated as 'some believe it belonged to the earliest church'; confirm fair to both.
Practice of tongues varies between Pentecostal congregations; stated as 'some praying in tongues'. Confirm.
Testimony example 'a night they didn't drink' and the hook scene are illustrative; confirm tone.
'Pentecostal churches take their name from a day in the book of Acts': the name comes from the day of Pentecost in Acts 2; confirm.
Original: πνεῦμα in John 3:8 (τὸ πνεῦμα ὅπου θέλει πνεῖ … ἐκ τοῦ πνεύματος); the wind/Spirit wordplay is standard; confirm.
Audit (2026-10-02): Acts 2:1–2 says 'in one place' and 'all the house', not 'one room'; teach and fork corrected. Acts 2:2, 2:4, Psalm 150:6 and John 3:8 checked exact.
